properties.title: Spanish New Mexico c. 1760
properties.label: New Mexico
properties.description: Spanish New Mexico was a ribbon of Hispanic villages and Pueblo towns along the upper Rio Grande from Taos to Albuquerque, linked by the Camino Real across the waterless Jornada del Muerto to the El Paso district, which also belonged to the province. All around it lay the lands of independent Apache, Navajo, Ute and Comanche peoples, with whom New Mexicans traded, fought and intermarried. The Hopi pueblos to the west stayed outside Spanish control after 1680.
properties.note: A hand-drawn outline of the settled corridor, after the maps in Gerhard (The North Frontier of New Spain) and Kessell. It includes Acoma and Laguna but not Zuni or Hopi. The Jornada del Muerto, between Socorro and El Paso, had no permanent settlement.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).

properties.title: Province of Texas c. 1760
properties.label: Texas
properties.description: The Spanish province of Texas (the Nuevas Filipinas) ran from the Medina and Nueces rivers in the southwest to the Arroyo Hondo near the French post of Natchitoches, its capital at Los Adaes on the Louisiana border. Its Spanish population, a few thousand at most, lived in a handful of places: San Antonio, La Bahía, and the missions and presidio of East Texas, strung along the Camino Real de los Tejas. The rest was Caddo, Apache, Comanche, Wichita, Karankawa and other Native country.
properties.note: A schematic outline after Chipman and the Handbook of Texas. The boundaries with Coahuila (the Medina River) and with Nuevo Santander (the Nueces) were set in the 1720s–50s; the northern limit was undefined. The coast is clipped to the modern shoreline.

sources.citation: Donald E. Chipman and Harriett Denise Joseph, Spanish Texas, 1519–1821, rev. ed. (University of Texas Press, 2010).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Boundaries".
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Jesuit California c. 1760
properties.label: Jesuit California
properties.description: From Loreto (1697) the Jesuits built a chain of about seventeen missions down to the Cape and north up the peninsula, governing it almost as a private domain, with a small garrison paid for out of donations (the Pious Fund) as much as by the Crown. The missions depended on supplies shipped across the Gulf from Sonora and Sinaloa, and epidemics devastated the Cochimí, Guaycura and Pericú peoples they gathered. The Jesuits were expelled in 1767–68, just before the advance into Alta California.
properties.note: Drawn as the modern state of Baja California Sur, which roughly matches the extent of the missions in 1760. The northernmost mission, Santa Gertrudis (1752), stood just north of the present state line, and San Borja followed in 1762.

sources.citation: Harry W. Crosby, Antigua California: Mission and Colony on the Peninsular Frontier, 1697–1768 (University of New Mexico Press, 1994).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Nuevo Santander (1748–1755)
properties.label: Nuevo Santander
properties.description: The coastal plain between Pánuco and Texas, long held by unconquered peoples, was colonised in a single planned campaign by José de Escandón, who founded about two dozen towns and missions with settlers from Querétaro, Nuevo León and Coahuila between 1748 and 1755. Unlike most of the north, Nuevo Santander was settled by ranching families rather than miners or missionaries, and its towns on the Rio Grande (Camargo, Reynosa, Mier, Revilla, Laredo) became the base of the later Tamaulipas–Texas borderland.
properties.note: Drawn as the modern state of Tamaulipas. The colony also extended north of the Rio Grande to the Nueces River (including Laredo), which is not shown, and its southern edge with the Huasteca differed from the modern line.

sources.citation: Patricia Osante, Orígenes del Nuevo Santander (1748–1772) (UNAM / Universidad Autónoma de Tamaulipas, 1997).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Sebastián Vizcaíno's voyage up the California coast
properties.label: Vizcaíno 1602–03
properties.description: To find a harbour where the returning Manila galleons could refit, Sebastián Vizcaíno sailed from Acapulco with three ships and charted the coast of the Californias, giving their present names to the bays of San Diego and Monterey, which he praised extravagantly. His descriptions and charts guided Spanish navigators for a century and a half, and Monterey became the goal of the expeditions of 1769. No harbour was settled in his time.
properties.note: Main landfalls only: Cabo San Lucas, Bahía Magdalena (schematic), the outer coast of Baja California (schematic), San Diego (November 1602) and Monterey (December 1602). Part of the expedition went on north toward Cape Mendocino in January 1603.

sources.citation: W. Michael Mathes, Vizcaíno and Spanish Expansion in the Pacific Ocean, 1580–1630 (California Historical Society, 1968).
William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (E. P. Dutton, 1939).

properties.title: Acapulco: the galleon fair and Fort San Diego
properties.label: Acapulco fair
properties.description: When the Manila galleon arrived, usually in the winter, merchants from Mexico City and as far as Peru came down the mountain road to the fair at Acapulco to buy silk, porcelain, cotton cloth and spices for silver; for the rest of the year the hot port was nearly empty. The Fort of San Diego, built in 1615–17 after Dutch raids in the Pacific, guarded the bay and the galleons.
properties.note: Marked at the Fuerte de San Diego. The present pentagonal fort is a rebuilding after the earthquake of 1776.

sources.citation: William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (E. P. Dutton, 1939).
Peter Gerhard, Pirates on the West Coast of New Spain, 1575–1742 (Arthur H. Clark, 1960; repr. as Pirates of New Spain, 1575–1742, Dover, 2003).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: The Desagüe of Huehuetoca and the Nochistongo cut
properties.label: Desagüe (Nochistongo)
properties.description: After the floods of 1604 and 1607 the viceregal government adopted the engineer and printer Enrico Martínez's plan to drain the basin to the north: a canal took the Cuautitlán River, the main source of Lake Zumpango, past Huehuetoca and through a tunnel of some 6–7 km under the hills of Nochistongo into the valley of the Tula River, which drains to the Gulf by way of the Pánuco. Thousands of Indigenous labourers drafted from the basin dug the tunnel in 1607–09, but it kept caving in; from 1637 it was turned into an enormous open cut, the Tajo de Nochistongo, finished only in 1789. The Desagüe was the largest public work of the colony and began the long drainage of the lakes.
properties.note: Schematic line from Cuautitlán past Huehuetoca and through the Nochistongo hills to El Salto (Tepeji del Río, Hidalgo), where the drained water entered the Tula valley. The tunnel and later cut ran northwest from near Huehuetoca; the exact alignment is not drawn from a survey. The end date (1789, completion of the open cut) lies outside the era by design. Sources give 28, 29 or 30 November 1607 for the start of work; only the month is shown. Gillingham (ch. 7), following Candiani, puts the Indigenous workforce drafted for the first works at 60,000 and the tunnel at about seven kilometres.

sources.citation: Vera S. Candiani, Dreaming of Dry Land: Environmental Transformation in Colonial Mexico City (Stanford University Press, 2014).
Louisa Schell Hoberman, "Bureaucracy and Disaster: Mexico City and the Flood of 1629", Journal of Latin American Studies 6, no. 2 (1974): 211–230.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 7.

properties.title: The great flood of Mexico City
properties.label: Flood of 1629
properties.description: After days of torrential rain in September 1629, with the drainage tunnel blocked, the lakes rose over Mexico City and much of it stayed under water for about five years. Thousands died or left, people moved about by canoe, and the Crown considered moving the capital to higher ground. Martínez was briefly jailed, and the disaster committed the government to the costly, centuries-long Desagüe.
properties.note: Marked at the Zócalo; the flood covered most of the city.

sources.citation: Louisa Schell Hoberman, "Bureaucracy and Disaster: Mexico City and the Flood of 1629", Journal of Latin American Studies 6, no. 2 (1974): 211–230.
Vera S. Candiani, Dreaming of Dry Land: Environmental Transformation in Colonial Mexico City (Stanford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: The alleged Black conspiracy of 1612
properties.label: Conspiracy of 1612
properties.description: Late in 1611 some 1,500 Black and mulatto residents of Mexico City marched to the viceroy's palace with the body of an enslaved woman beaten to death by her owner. Rumours followed of a plot to rise at Easter 1612, kill the Spaniards and crown a king, and after interrogations the Audiencia had 35 Black and mulatto men and women hanged in the main square on 2 May. A curfew and travel controls on people of African descent followed; whether there was any plot at all is doubted.
properties.note: Marked at the cathedral; the gallows stood in the main square facing the cathedral and the palace. Gillingham (ch. 7) also mentions alleged conspiracies of 1608 and 1611, which are not mapped.

sources.citation: María Elena Martínez, "The Black Blood of New Spain: Limpieza de Sangre, Racial Violence, and Gendered Power in Early Colonial Mexico", William and Mary Quarterly 61, no. 3 (2004): 479–520.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 7.

properties.title: Yanga's maroon settlement
properties.label: Yanga
properties.description: Runaway slaves led by Yanga held a fortified settlement in the mountains above the Veracruz–Puebla road and raided the traffic of the main highway to the coast. A force of about 550 men sent from Puebla in 1609 burned the settlement but could not defeat the maroons, and the viceroyalty eventually agreed to recognise a free town in return for loyalty, a Franciscan priest and a promise to return future runaways. San Lorenzo de los Negros, founded by about 1630 near Córdoba, is the modern town of Yanga.
properties.note: Marked at the modern town of Yanga (renamed in 1932); the palenque of 1609 lay in the mountains nearby, and San Lorenzo itself moved more than once. The date of the agreement is given as 1618 or later, and of the town's formal recognition anywhere up to the 1630s. Gillingham (ch. 7) does not name Yanga, but describes a runaway settlement "near Puebla" allowed to survive on condition that it took in no more runaways.

sources.citation: David M. Davidson, "Negro Slave Control and Resistance in Colonial Mexico, 1519–1650", Hispanic American Historical Review 46, no. 3 (1966): 235–253.

Frank T. Proctor III, "Slave Rebellion and Liberty in Colonial Mexico", in Ben Vinson III and Matthew Restall, eds., Black Mexico: Race and Society from Colonial to Modern Times (University of New Mexico Press, 2009).
Wikipedia, "Gaspar Yanga".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 7.

properties.title: Guillén Lombardo's independence plot
properties.label: Lombardo 1642
properties.description: William Lamport, an Irish adventurer known in Mexico as Guillén Lombardo de Guzmán, was arrested on 26 October 1642 with papers for a plan to oust the viceroy with forged royal orders, proclaim himself king of an independent Mexico and give equal rights to creoles, Indigenous people and Blacks who joined him. He found no followers. He spent seventeen years in the cells of the Inquisition, escaped briefly in 1650, and died at the stake in the auto de fe of November 1659. The plot is remembered as the first project for Mexican independence, but its failure shows how firmly the viceregal order was accepted.
properties.note: Marked at the palace of the Inquisition on the Plaza de Santo Domingo (now the Palacio de la Escuela de Medicina), where he was held; the present building dates from the 1730s. Accounts say he strangled himself on his iron collar before the fire reached him.
properties.modern_place: Palacio de la Escuela de Medicina, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Ryan Dominic Crewe, "Brave New Spain: An Irishman's Independence Plot in Seventeenth-Century Mexico", Past & Present 207 (2010): 53–87.
Wikipedia, "William Lamport".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: The riot of 1624 against Viceroy Gelves
properties.label: Riot of 1624
properties.description: A long conflict between the reforming viceroy, the Marqués de Gelves, and Archbishop Pérez de la Serna, who had excommunicated him, ended when a crowd stirred up by the archbishop's party attacked and burned part of the viceregal palace. The rioters cheered the king even as they attacked his viceroy; Gelves escaped in disguise and was replaced, and the crowd was punished only lightly. The riot showed the power of the Creole elite and the clergy against the viceroy.

sources.citation: J. I. Israel, Race, Class and Politics in Colonial Mexico, 1610–1670 (Oxford University Press, 1975).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 5, 7 and 8.

properties.title: The corn riot of 1692
properties.label: Riot of 1692
properties.description: After floods and a crop blight drove up the price of maize, a crowd of Indigenous and mixed-race city dwellers gathered at the public granary, then attacked and burned the viceregal palace, the town hall and the market stalls of the main square. The authorities blamed the Indigenous population, banned pulque for a time and tried to make Indigenous people live in their own barrios, separate from Spaniards.
properties.note: Marked at the town hall (Antiguo Palacio del Ayuntamiento) on the main square, one of the buildings burned. Gillingham gives two triggers: the death of a woman in the hungry crowd at the granary (ch. 8) and the beating to death of an Indigenous woman (ch. 7). He reads the riot, as Cope and Sigüenza y Góngora did, as a rising of the city's multiracial poor (the "plebe"), and counts twelve rioters executed afterwards.
properties.modern_place: Antiguo Palacio del Ayuntamiento, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: R. Douglas Cope, The Limits of Racial Domination: Plebeian Society in Colonial Mexico City, 1660–1720 (University of Wisconsin Press, 1994).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 7 and 8.

properties.title: The cult of the Virgin of Guadalupe at Tepeyac
properties.label: Guadalupe
properties.description: The image of the Virgin at the shrine of Tepeyac, north of Mexico City, was said to have appeared in 1531, but the cult spread across New Spain only after Miguel Sánchez published the apparition story in 1648 and Luis Lasso de la Vega a Nahuatl version in 1649. A larger church was consecrated in 1709. When an epidemic (matlazahuatl) killed some 40,000 people in the capital in 1736–37, the city swore the Virgin as its patron, and New Spain as a whole followed in 1746, confirmed by the pope in 1754. She became the emblem of creole patriotism and later of the insurgents of 1810.
properties.note: Marked at the old basilica of 1709 (now the Templo Expiatorio a Cristo Rey). The death toll of 40,157 given by Gillingham (ch. 2) is the contemporary count published by Cabrera y Quintero; modern studies date the epidemic 1736–39 across New Spain.
properties.modern_place: Antigua Basílica de Guadalupe, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Stafford Poole, Our Lady of Guadalupe: The Origins and Sources of a Mexican National Symbol, 1531–1797 (University of Arizona Press, 1995).
D. A. Brading, Mexican Phoenix: Our Lady of Guadalupe: Image and Tradition across Five Centuries (Cambridge University Press, 2001).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 2 and 3.

properties.title: Santa Fe founded
properties.label: Santa Fe
properties.description: Governor Pedro de Peralta moved the capital of New Mexico from San Gabriel to a new villa at the foot of the Sangre de Cristo mountains, laid out around a plaza with the Casas Reales (now the Palace of the Governors) on its north side. For most of the seventeenth century New Mexico was a Franciscan mission field with a few hundred Spanish settlers, supplied by wagon train from Mexico City every three years or so.
properties.note: Marked at the Palace of the Governors. Some sources date the first Spanish settlement at Santa Fe to 1607–08.
properties.modern_place: Palace of the Governors, Santa Fe

sources.citation: John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).
US National Park Service, El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro National Historic Trail, "History & Culture".
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 3.

properties.title: The Pueblo Revolt and the siege of Santa Fe
properties.label: Pueblo Revolt 1680
properties.description: Coordinated from Taos by Po'pay, a Tewa leader from Ohkay Owingeh, with knotted cords carried by runners to count the days, the Pueblos rose together against Franciscan suppression of their religion, forced labour and tribute, after years of drought and Apache raids. They killed about 400 colonists and 21 of the 33 friars and besieged Governor Antonio de Otermín in the Casas Reales at Santa Fe. On 21 August the survivors abandoned the city. It was the most successful Native rising against Spanish rule in North America.
properties.note: The rising broke out across the pueblos at once; the point marks the siege of Santa Fe.
properties.modern_place: Palace of the Governors, Santa Fe

sources.citation: Andrew L. Knaut, The Pueblo Revolt of 1680: Conquest and Resistance in Seventeenth-Century New Mexico (University of Oklahoma Press, 1995).
John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 7 and 8.

properties.title: Retreat from New Mexico to El Paso
properties.label: Retreat 1680
properties.description: Otermín led about a thousand survivors down the Rio Grande, finding the downriver Spanish settlers already gone ahead from Isleta, and reached the mission of Guadalupe at El Paso del Norte in the autumn. For twelve years the colony lived in exile at El Paso, and Piro and Tiwa people who had come south with the Spaniards founded the communities of Ysleta and Socorro there.
properties.note: Main stops only, along the Camino Real.

sources.citation: Andrew L. Knaut, The Pueblo Revolt of 1680: Conquest and Resistance in Seventeenth-Century New Mexico (University of Oklahoma Press, 1995).
John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).

properties.title: El Paso del Norte: mission of Guadalupe
properties.label: El Paso del Norte
properties.description: Franciscans founded the mission of Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe among the Manso people at the pass where the Camino Real crossed the Rio Grande. After 1680 it became the refuge and temporary capital of New Mexico, and grew into the largest settlement on the road between Chihuahua and Santa Fe (modern Ciudad Juárez).
properties.note: Marked at the mission church, which still stands beside the cathedral of Ciudad Juárez.
properties.modern_place: Misión de Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe, Ciudad Juárez

sources.citation: John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).
US National Park Service, El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro National Historic Trail, "History & Culture".

properties.title: Diego de Vargas reoccupies Santa Fe
properties.label: Vargas 1692–93
properties.description: Governor Diego de Vargas marched north from El Paso in 1692 and took ceremonial possession of Santa Fe, with the Pueblos agreeing to submit largely without fighting. When he returned with colonists in late 1693 the Tanos holding Santa Fe refused to leave, and he took the town by force and executed about seventy of its defenders. A last Pueblo rising in 1696 failed. Afterwards Spanish rule was less harsh: the encomienda was not restored, and Pueblos and Spaniards became allies against the Apaches and Comanches.

sources.citation: John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Albuquerque founded
properties.label: Albuquerque
properties.description: Governor Francisco Cuervo y Valdés founded the Villa de San Francisco Xavier de Alburquerque on the Rio Grande in the farmland of the Río Abajo, naming it after the viceroy, the Duque de Alburquerque. With Santa Fe and Santa Cruz de la Cañada it was one of the three Spanish villas of New Mexico.
properties.note: Marked at Old Town, the colonial plaza.

sources.citation: John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).

properties.title: Jesuit missions among the Yaquis
properties.label: Yaqui missions
properties.description: The Yaquis had defeated Spanish expeditions, but in 1610 they made peace and asked for missionaries, and in 1617 Jesuits led by Andrés Pérez de Ribas began gathering the Yaqui population into eight mission towns along the lower Río Yaqui, among them Tórim. The Yaqui towns became the largest Jesuit mission field in the northwest, and the base for missions further north into Sonora. In 1740 the Yaquis and Mayos rose against the missions and settlers in a revolt that spread across southern Sonora.
properties.note: Marked at Tórim, one of the eight towns.

sources.citation: Andrés Pérez de Ribas, History of the Triumphs of Our Holy Faith amongst the Most Barbarous and Fierce Peoples of the New World (1645), trans. Daniel T. Reff, Maureen Ahern and Richard K. Danford (University of Arizona Press, 1999).
Edward H. Spicer, Cycles of Conquest: The Impact of Spain, Mexico, and the United States on the Indians of the Southwest, 1533–1960 (University of Arizona Press, 1962).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: The Yaqui and Mayo revolt of 1740
properties.label: Yaqui revolt 1740
properties.description: After a failed harvest in 1739 and floods in 1740 brought famine to the mission towns of the lower Yaqui and Mayo rivers, long-standing grievances over the Jesuits' control of mission land and produce and over forced labour in the mines broke into revolt. Two Yaqui leaders, Muni of Ráhum and Bernabé of Huírivis, took their complaints to Mexico City, but while they were away rebels under Juan Calixto, joined by Mayos and Lower Pimas, took the river towns and drove missionaries and settlers to the mining town of Álamos. Agustín de Vildósola defeated the rebels in the second half of 1740 and a pardon was offered, but Muni and Bernabé were executed at Buenavista on 23 June 1741. The rising ended the Jesuits' unchallenged rule over the Yaqui towns and opened them to settlers and soldiers.
properties.note: Marked at Ráhum, one of the eight Yaqui towns and home of Muni and Calixto; the revolt spread along the Yaqui, Mayo and Fuerte rivers. The start is given only to the year: sources describe scattered outbreaks in the Mayo and Lower Pima country in early 1740. The execution date is from a Jesuit letter of July 1741 summarised in the University of Arizona mission records. Casualty figures in the literature (up to a thousand settlers and several thousand Indigenous people) are not used. Gillingham (ch. 8) ranks it with the Pueblo Revolt as one of the two great frontier wars of the colony.

sources.citation: Evelyn Hu-DeHart, Missionaries, Miners, and Indians: Spanish Contact with the Yaqui Nation of Northwestern New Spain, 1533–1820 (University of Arizona Press, 1981).
John D. Meredith, "The Yaqui Rebellion of 1740: A Jesuit Account and Its Implications", Ethnohistory 22, no. 3 (1975): 222–261.
Edward H. Spicer, Cycles of Conquest: The Impact of Spain, Mexico, and the United States on the Indians of the Southwest, 1533–1960 (University of Arizona Press, 1962).

University of Arizona, Mission 2000 / Documentary Relations of the Southwest catalogue, document summaries for 1740–42 (letters of Lorenzo Joseph García, Torim, 14 July 1741, and Agustín de Arriola, Huirivis, 12 October 1741).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: Kino founds Nuestra Señora de los Dolores
properties.label: Kino at Dolores
properties.description: The Tyrolean Jesuit Eusebio Francisco Kino founded the mission of Dolores at Cosari in the upper San Miguel valley, his base for 24 years of exploring and founding missions across the Pimería Alta (northern Sonora and southern Arizona). Introducing cattle, wheat and fruit trees to the O'odham, he made more than forty journeys, reaching the Gila and the Colorado, and by 1701–02 had convinced himself and his superiors that California was a peninsula, not an island. He died at Magdalena in 1711.
properties.note: The mission ruins lie on a hill above the San Miguel River, roughly 18–30 km north of Cucurpe (sources differ). The point is schematic and has no geocoded check.

sources.citation: Herbert Eugene Bolton, Rim of Christendom: A Biography of Eusebio Francisco Kino, Pacific Coast Pioneer (Macmillan, 1936).
Edward H. Spicer, Cycles of Conquest: The Impact of Spain, Mexico, and the United States on the Indians of the Southwest, 1533–1960 (University of Arizona Press, 1962).

properties.title: Mission San Xavier del Bac
properties.label: San Xavier del Bac
properties.description: Kino visited the large O'odham village of Bac on the Santa Cruz River in 1692 and laid the foundations of a church in 1700. It was the northernmost mission of the Pimería Alta for most of the century. The present church was built by Franciscans in 1783–97.

sources.citation: Herbert Eugene Bolton, Rim of Christendom: A Biography of Eusebio Francisco Kino, Pacific Coast Pioneer (Macmillan, 1936).
John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).

properties.title: The Pima revolt of 1751
properties.label: Pima revolt 1751
properties.description: Luis Oacpicagigua of Sáric, a Pima captain-general named by the Spaniards, led a rising of the O'odham of the Pimería Alta in which more than a hundred settlers and two Jesuits were killed. It was put down within months, and the Spaniards responded by founding a presidio at Tubac (1752), the first in what is now Arizona.

sources.citation: Edward H. Spicer, Cycles of Conquest: The Impact of Spain, Mexico, and the United States on the Indians of the Southwest, 1533–1960 (University of Arizona Press, 1962).
John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).

properties.title: Presidio of Tubac
properties.label: Tubac
properties.description: Founded after the Pima revolt on the Santa Cruz River, near the mission of Tumacácori, to guard the northern Pimería against the O'odham and the Apaches. In 1774–75 its captain Juan Bautista de Anza set out from here to open an overland route to Alta California.

sources.citation: John L. Kessell, Spain in the Southwest: A Narrative History of Colonial New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, and California (University of Oklahoma Press, 2002).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Loreto: the Jesuits reach California
properties.label: Loreto 1697
properties.description: After repeated failed attempts to settle California, the Crown let the Jesuits try at their own expense. Juan María de Salvatierra landed on the Gulf shore with a handful of soldiers and founded the mission of Nuestra Señora de Loreto, which became the capital of the Californias until 1777. Supplies came by boat from the Sonoran and Sinaloan missions across the Gulf.

sources.citation: Harry W. Crosby, Antigua California: Mission and Colony on the Peninsular Frontier, 1697–1768 (University of New Mexico Press, 1994).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: San José del Cabo: a landfall for the Manila galleon
properties.label: San José del Cabo
properties.description: After months at sea, the galleons from Manila first sighted land off California, but for over a century and a half Spain had no port on that coast where they could take on water and fresh food against scurvy. In 1730 the Jesuit Nicolás Tamaral founded the mission of San José del Cabo beside the fresh-water estuary near the tip of the peninsula, which the galleons could use. It was destroyed in the Pericú revolt of 1734 and refounded with a garrison. In 1769 French, Spanish and Mexican astronomers observed the transit of Venus here.
properties.note: Marked at the modern town; the mission stood beside the estuary of the Río San José. Gillingham (ch. 6) dates the first Spanish port on the California coast to 1730 and mentions a Pericú attack on a galleon.
properties.modern_place: San José del Cabo, Baja California Sur, Mexico

sources.citation: Harry W. Crosby, Antigua California: Mission and Colony on the Peninsular Frontier, 1697–1768 (University of New Mexico Press, 1994).

Doyce B. Nunis Jr., ed., The 1769 Transit of Venus: The Baja California Observations of Jean-Baptiste Chappe d'Auteroche, Vicente de Doz, and Joaquín Velázquez Cárdenas de León (Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, 1982).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 6 and 8.

properties.title: The Pericú revolt in the Cape region
properties.label: Pericú revolt 1734
properties.description: The Pericú and Guaycura of the southern peninsula, resisting the missionaries' attacks on polygamy and their own leaders, rose and killed the Jesuits Lorenzo Carranco at Santiago and Nicolás Tamaral at San José del Cabo, and burned the southern missions. Troops from Sinaloa restored control by 1737, and a presidio was built at San José del Cabo to protect the galleons' landfall. Disease reduced the Pericú to a remnant within a few decades.
properties.note: Marked at Santiago, where the revolt began; the attacks extended to La Paz and San José del Cabo.

sources.citation: Harry W. Crosby, Antigua California: Mission and Colony on the Peninsular Frontier, 1697–1768 (University of New Mexico Press, 1994).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: The Tepehuán revolt
properties.label: Tepehuán revolt 1616
properties.description: Inspired by a prophet who promised to restore the old order, the Tepehuanes of the Durango sierra attacked the missions, mines and ranches of Nueva Vizcaya, killing eight Jesuits and hundreds of Spanish settlers and their African and Indigenous servants, beginning near Santa Catalina de Tepehuanes. The war lasted until about 1620, and the province took years to recover.
properties.note: Marked at Santa Catarina de Tepehuanes, where the first attack fell. Killings also took place at Santiago Papasquiaro, Zape and elsewhere. Gillingham (ch. 3) dates the rising to 1617 and 1618 and places it in Chihuahua; it broke out in November 1616 in the Durango sierra (Gradie, Deeds).

sources.citation: Charlotte M. Gradie, The Tepehuan Revolt of 1616: Militarism, Evangelism, and Colonialism in Seventeenth-Century Nueva Vizcaya (University of Utah Press, 2000).
Susan M. Deeds, Defiance and Deference in Mexico's Colonial North: Indians under Spanish Rule in Nueva Vizcaya (University of Texas Press, 2003).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 3.

properties.title: Silver at Parral
properties.label: Parral 1631
properties.description: A silver strike at San José del Parral, near Santa Bárbara, set off the great boom of the seventeenth-century north. Parral became the largest town of Nueva Vizcaya and the usual seat of its governors, and its demand for food, mules and labour drew ranches, farms and labour drafts from the Conchos and Tarahumara missions.
properties.note: The strike is usually dated 1631 (some sources say 1629); Gillingham (ch. 6) gives 1623. The date shown follows West.

sources.citation: Robert C. West, The Mining Community in Northern New Spain: The Parral Mining District (University of California Press, 1949).
Susan M. Deeds, Defiance and Deference in Mexico's Colonial North: Indians under Spanish Rule in Nueva Vizcaya (University of Texas Press, 2003).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: The Tarahumara revolts
properties.label: Tarahumara revolts
properties.description: As Jesuit missions and Spanish ranchers moved into the upper Papigochi valley, Tarahumara (Rarámuri) communities rose repeatedly: in 1648, in 1650, when the Jesuit at Papigochi was killed, and in 1652–53 under Teporaca, who was captured and hanged in March 1653; the Spanish town of Villa de Aguilar, founded nearby to hold the valley, did not survive the wars. Further risings followed in 1690 and 1696–98. Many Rarámuri withdrew into the barrancas of the Sierra Madre, where they kept much of their independence.
properties.note: Marked at Ciudad Guerrero (Vicente Guerrero), the site of the mission of Papigochi. The Villa de Aguilar is placed at Basúchil, about 8 km to the southeast.

sources.citation: Susan M. Deeds, Defiance and Deference in Mexico's Colonial North: Indians under Spanish Rule in Nueva Vizcaya (University of Texas Press, 2003).
Edward H. Spicer, Cycles of Conquest: The Impact of Spain, Mexico, and the United States on the Indians of the Southwest, 1533–1960 (University of Arizona Press, 1962).

properties.title: Chihuahua founded
properties.label: Chihuahua
properties.description: After rich silver finds at nearby Santa Eulalia, the Real de San Francisco de Cuéllar was founded on the Chuvíscar River in 1709 and made a villa, San Felipe el Real, in 1718. It overtook Parral as the main town of Nueva Vizcaya and the hub of the Camino Real between Durango and El Paso.

sources.citation: Robert C. West, The Mining Community in Northern New Spain: The Parral Mining District (University of California Press, 1949).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: La Salle's Fort Saint-Louis
properties.label: Fort Saint-Louis
properties.description: René-Robert Cavelier de La Salle, aiming for the mouth of the Mississippi, landed his French colony on Matagorda Bay instead in 1685 and built a settlement on Garcitas Creek. La Salle was murdered by his own men in 1687, and Karankawas destroyed the settlement, probably around Christmas 1688. News of the French alarmed New Spain, and the search for them, which ended when Alonso de León found the ruins in April 1689, began Spanish settlement in Texas.
properties.note: Coordinates of the excavated site on Garcitas Creek from Wikipedia. The geocoder finds a marker of the same name at Inez, about 19 km to the north, so a distance of that size is expected. The name "Fort St. Louis" is a later one; the colonists called it only the habitation near the baie Saint-Louis.
properties.modern_place: Fort St. Louis, Victoria County, Texas

sources.citation: Donald E. Chipman and Harriett Denise Joseph, Spanish Texas, 1519–1821, rev. ed. (University of Texas Press, 2010).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "La Salle's Texas Settlement".

properties.title: Monclova, capital of Coahuila
properties.label: Monclova
properties.description: Alonso de León, governor of the new province of Coahuila, founded Santiago de la Monclova on the site of an earlier settlement as its capital and the starting point for the expeditions into Texas. Coahuila's missions and presidios formed the base from which Texas was supplied.
properties.note: A first settlement on the site dates from the 1570s; the date given is León's refounding.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Donald E. Chipman and Harriett Denise Joseph, Spanish Texas, 1519–1821, rev. ed. (University of Texas Press, 2010).

properties.title: Mission San Francisco de los Tejas
properties.label: San Francisco de los Tejas
properties.description: The first Spanish mission in East Texas was founded among the Hasinai Caddo, whom the Spaniards called Tejas ("friends"), giving the province its name. Epidemics, drought and Caddo hostility led the friars to abandon it in 1693, and Spain left Texas for more than twenty years.
properties.note: Marked at Mission Tejas State Park, near Weches. The site has not been found; the Handbook of Texas places it on San Pedro Creek a few kilometres west of the park.

sources.citation: Donald E. Chipman and Harriett Denise Joseph, Spanish Texas, 1519–1821, rev. ed. (University of Texas Press, 2010).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "San Francisco de los Tejas Mission".
US National Park Service, El Camino Real de los Tejas National Historic Trail, "History & Culture".

properties.title: San Juan Bautista del Río Grande
properties.label: San Juan Bautista
properties.description: A mission founded in 1699 and moved in 1700 to a site near the fords of the Rio Grande, soon joined by two more missions and a presidio. Called the "gateway to Spanish Texas", it was the last Spanish base before the crossing, and in 1714 the French trader Louis Juchereau de St. Denis arrived here from Louisiana, prompting Spain to reoccupy East Texas.
properties.note: Marked at Guerrero, Coahuila; the mission ruins are just outside the town. The date is the move to this site (1 January 1700 by most accounts).

sources.citation: Donald E. Chipman and Harriett Denise Joseph, Spanish Texas, 1519–1821, rev. ed. (University of Texas Press, 2010).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "San Juan Bautista".

properties.title: Camino Real de los Tejas
properties.label: Camino Real de los Tejas
properties.description: The road from Saltillo and Monclova across the Rio Grande to San Antonio and on to the missions of East Texas and the capital at Los Adaes. It followed older Native trails and had many variants as river crossings and dangers changed. Along it moved soldiers, friars, livestock and the contraband trade with French Louisiana on which Los Adaes depended.
properties.note: Main stops only; the stretch between San Antonio and Nacogdoches (two schematic vertices, near the Colorado and the Trinity crossings) had several alternative routes.

sources.citation: US National Park Service, El Camino Real de los Tejas National Historic Trail, "History & Culture".
Donald E. Chipman and Harriett Denise Joseph, Spanish Texas, 1519–1821, rev. ed. (University of Texas Press, 2010).

properties.title: Spain returns to East Texas
properties.label: East Texas missions 1716
properties.description: In response to French traders from Louisiana, an expedition under Domingo Ramón, guided by St. Denis, founded four missions among the Caddo in 1716, among them Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe at the site of Nacogdoches, with a presidio to guard them. In 1717 Fray Antonio Margil added two more further east, Dolores de los Ais at San Augustine and San Miguel de los Adaes. They gained few converts but held the border against France.
properties.note: Marked at Nacogdoches; the missions were scattered between the Neches River and Los Adaes.

sources.citation: Donald E. Chipman and Harriett Denise Joseph, Spanish Texas, 1519–1821, rev. ed. (University of Texas Press, 2010).
US National Park Service, El Camino Real de los Tejas National Historic Trail, "History & Culture".

properties.title: San Antonio founded
properties.label: San Antonio
properties.description: Martín de Alarcón founded the mission of San Antonio de Valero (later called the Alamo) and the presidio of San Antonio de Béxar at the springs of the San Antonio River, as a halfway station between the Rio Grande and East Texas. Settlers from the Canary Islands founded the villa of San Fernando here in 1731, and five missions lined the river, making San Antonio the largest settlement in Texas.
properties.note: Marked at the Alamo. The mission was founded on 1 May and the presidio on 5 May 1718; both were moved short distances in their early years.

sources.citation: Donald E. Chipman and Harriett Denise Joseph, Spanish Texas, 1519–1821, rev. ed. (University of Texas Press, 2010).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "San Antonio de Valero Mission".

properties.title: Los Adaes, capital of Texas
properties.label: Los Adaes
properties.description: After a French raid in 1719 drove the Spaniards out of East Texas, the Marqués de San Miguel de Aguayo, a Coahuila landowner whose family's estates became some of the largest in the Americas, led a large expedition in 1721 that restored the missions and built the presidio of Nuestra Señora del Pilar de Los Adaes, about 20 km from the French post of Natchitoches. Los Adaes was the capital of Texas for half a century, the Spanish answer to the French on the frontier, and in practice it lived on trade with them.
properties.note: Dated to the founding of the presidio. Sources differ on when Los Adaes became the capital: from its founding in 1721, or formally under the presidio regulations of 1729. Its abandonment in 1772–73 belongs to the next era.

sources.citation: Donald E. Chipman and Harriett Denise Joseph, Spanish Texas, 1519–1821, rev. ed. (University of Texas Press, 2010).
US National Park Service, El Camino Real de los Tejas National Historic Trail, "History & Culture".
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Los Adaes".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: Destruction of the San Sabá mission
properties.label: San Sabá 1758
properties.description: The mission of Santa Cruz de San Sabá and the presidio of San Luis de las Amarillas were founded in 1757 for the Lipan Apaches on the San Saba River, far northwest of San Antonio. The Apaches never settled there, and a force of some 2,000 Comanches and allied Wichita and other nations, enemies of the Apaches, burned the mission and killed eight Spaniards. A punitive campaign under Diego Ortiz Parrilla was defeated at the fortified Wichita villages on the Red River in 1759. The episode marked the limit of Spanish power on the southern plains.
properties.note: Marked at the presidio near Menard; the mission stood a few kilometres downstream.

sources.citation: Robert S. Weddle, The San Sabá Mission: Spanish Pivot in Texas (University of Texas Press, 1964).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Santa Cruz de San Sabá Mission".
Donald E. Chipman and Harriett Denise Joseph, Spanish Texas, 1519–1821, rev. ed. (University of Texas Press, 2010).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Laredo founded
properties.label: Laredo
properties.description: Tomás Sánchez founded Villa de San Agustín de Laredo at a ford of the Rio Grande, the last and northernmost of Escandón's towns in Nuevo Santander. It sat on a crossing of the road to Texas.

sources.citation: Patricia Osante, Orígenes del Nuevo Santander (1748–1772) (UNAM / Universidad Autónoma de Tamaulipas, 1997).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Laredo, TX".

properties.title: Franciscan missions of the Sierra Gorda
properties.label: Sierra Gorda missions
properties.description: The Sierra Gorda, a rugged range only about 200 km from Mexico City, was a refuge of Pame and Jonaz peoples that resisted Spanish control for two centuries. After José de Escandón's campaigns of the 1740s, Franciscans of the College of San Fernando, including Junípero Serra (at Jalpan 1750–58), built five mission churches at Jalpan, Landa, Tilaco, Tancoyol and Concá, with richly carved façades made by Pame workers. Serra went on to found the missions of Alta California.
properties.note: Marked at the mission of Jalpan, the first and largest of the five (built 1751–58); the others (Concá, Tilaco, Tancoyol, Landa) were built between about 1754 and 1768 and lie within about 50 km.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Franciscan Missions in the Sierra Gorda of Querétaro" (inscribed 2003).
Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Puebla under Bishop Palafox
properties.label: Puebla
properties.description: Puebla was the second city of New Spain, a centre of textiles, wheat, soap and glazed pottery on the road between Veracruz and the capital. Its bishop Juan de Palafox y Mendoza, who was also briefly viceroy, completed and consecrated the cathedral in 1649 and gave his library to the seminary, the Biblioteca Palafoxiana; his clashes with the Jesuits divided the colony.
properties.note: Marked at the cathedral.

sources.citation: D. A. Brading, The First America: The Spanish Monarchy, Creole Patriots, and the Liberal State, 1492–1867 (Cambridge University Press, 1991).
J. I. Israel, Race, Class and Politics in Colonial Mexico, 1610–1670 (Oxford University Press, 1975).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 6 and 7.

properties.title: Querétaro and its aqueduct
properties.label: Querétaro
properties.description: Made a city in the mid-1650s, Querétaro grew rich in the eighteenth century as the gateway to the Bajío and the north, with large woollen workshops (obrajes) and the convents built by its merchants. Its great aqueduct of 74 arches, paid for largely by the Marqués de la Villa del Villar del Águila, brought spring water to the city.
properties.note: Marked at the aqueduct. Water reached the city in 1735 and the works were finished in 1738.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Valladolid (Morelia) and its cathedral
properties.label: Valladolid
properties.description: The episcopal city of Michoacán, whose bishopric stretched from the Pacific to the Bajío and San Luis Potosí. Its pink-stone baroque cathedral, begun in 1660 and finished in 1744, and the planned streets around it made Valladolid a model of the colonial provincial capital.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Guadalajara, capital of the west
properties.label: Guadalajara
properties.description: The seat of the audiencia and bishopric of Nueva Galicia, whose jurisdiction reached north to the mines of Zacatecas and the missions of Sinaloa. Its cathedral was completed in 1618. Merchants of Guadalajara competed with those of Mexico City for the trade of the north and the Pacific coast.
properties.note: Marked at the cathedral.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Conquest of the Nayar
properties.label: Nayar 1722
properties.description: In the deep canyons of the Sierra Madre between Nueva Galicia and Nueva Vizcaya, the Cora (Náayeri) kept an independent kingdom centred on a sacred mesa for two centuries after the conquest, surrounded by Spanish provinces. In January 1722 Juan Flores de San Pedro, with some 560 soldiers and Indigenous allies, stormed the Mesa del Nayar; the Cora leader, the Tonati, surrendered weeks later, and Jesuit missions were set up in the sierra. It was among the last unconquered enclaves in the core of New Spain.
properties.note: Marked at the village of Mesa del Nayar, using Wikipedia's coordinates; the geocoder's "Mesa del Nayar" is about 33 km to the west and is not used. The exact day of the assault is not given in the sources checked. Some sources call the commander Juan Flores de la Torre.
properties.modern_place: Mesa del Nayar, Del Nayar, Nayarit, Mexico

sources.citation: Raquel E. Güereca Durán, Caciques, intérpretes y soldados fronterizos: actores indígenas en la conquista del Nayar, siglo XVIII (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas, 2022).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 1 and 7.

properties.title: Antequera (Oaxaca) and the cochineal trade
properties.label: Oaxaca cochineal
properties.description: Cochineal, a red dye made from insects raised on nopal cactus by Mixtec and Zapotec households, was New Spain's most valuable export after silver. Merchants of Antequera and Mexico City, working through the district officials (alcaldes mayores) and the forced credit system of the repartimiento, bought it in the villages and shipped it through Veracruz to the textile industries of Europe.
properties.note: Marked at the cathedral of Oaxaca. Production was spread across the highland villages of the Mixteca and the Valley of Oaxaca.

sources.citation: Peter Gerhard, A Guide to the Historical Geography of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: The Cajonos riot and the Villa Alta idolatry campaign
properties.label: Cajonos 1700
properties.description: On 14 September 1700 two Zapotec church officials (fiscales) of San Francisco Cajonos, in the mountains of Villa Alta northeast of Antequera, led the Dominican friars to break up a traditional ritual. The next night a crowd stormed the friars' house and threatened to burn the church until the two men gave themselves up, and they were killed on a nearby hill. Fifteen rebels were later executed. In 1704–05 the new bishop of Oaxaca, Ángel Maldonado, offered the towns of Villa Alta a collective pardon in return for confessions, and their officials surrendered more than a hundred booklets of the 260-day ritual calendar and ritual songs, a rare record of the old religion kept alive in the sierra.
properties.note: Marked at San Francisco Cajonos. The killings are usually dated 16 September 1700. Gillingham (ch. 3) puts the pardoned population at 37,000 Zapotecs; Tavárez counts 104 towns, Zapotec, Mixe and Chinantec, with about 60,000 people, and 99 calendar booklets plus 4 of songs. The two dead were beatified in 2002 as the "martyrs of Cajonos".

sources.citation: David Tavárez, "Nicachi Songs: Zapotec Ritual Texts and Postclassic Ritual Knowledge in Colonial Oaxaca" (Foundation for the Advancement of Mesoamerican Studies, 2005).
David Tavárez, The Invisible War: Indigenous Devotions, Discipline, and Dissent in Colonial Mexico (Stanford University Press, 2011).
Wikipedia, "Martyrs of Cajonos".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 3.

properties.title: The Jalapa fair
properties.label: Jalapa fair
properties.description: To escape the deadly fevers of Veracruz, the Crown ordered the goods brought by the Spanish fleet to be sold at a fair in Jalapa (Xalapa), in the cooler hills on the road to the capital. Mexico City's great merchants dominated the fairs, buying European goods wholesale for resale throughout New Spain, until the last fleet sailed in 1776; the free-trade regulation of 1778 was extended to New Spain only in 1789.
properties.note: The fair was set up under the Proyecto of 1720 and formally fixed at Jalapa by a royal order of 1728; sources differ on whether the first was held in 1720 or 1721.

sources.citation: Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
D. A. Brading, The First America: The Spanish Monarchy, Creole Patriots, and the Liberal State, 1492–1867 (Cambridge University Press, 1991).

properties.title: Pirates sack Veracruz
properties.label: Sack of Veracruz 1683
properties.description: Buccaneers under Laurens de Graaf ("Lorencillo"), Nicholas van Hoorn and Michel de Grammont surprised Veracruz by night and held it for days, looting the city and locking thousands of residents in the churches. They left with a huge ransom and hundreds of enslaved captives. The raid exposed the weakness of the coastal defences and led to new fortifications.
properties.note: The attack began on the night of 17–18 May 1683; the pirates held the city and the nearby Isla de Sacrificios for several weeks in all.

sources.citation: Juan Juárez Moreno, Corsarios y piratas en Veracruz y Campeche (Escuela de Estudios Hispano-Americanos, 1972).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: Campeche: pirate raids and the city walls
properties.label: Campeche walls
properties.description: As Yucatán's port for logwood, salt and cloth, Campeche was raided repeatedly by English, French and Dutch buccaneers, notably in 1663 and in July 1685, when De Graaf and Grammont held it for weeks. From 1686 the city was enclosed by a hexagonal stone wall with eight bastions, finished in 1704, much of which still stands. English logwood cutters meanwhile settled on the Laguna de Términos and the coast of Belize.
properties.note: Marked at the Baluarte de la Soledad, one of the bastions. Gillingham (ch. 6) counts twelve attacks on Campeche between 1557 and 1708 and links them to the dye trade, which he calls indigo; the Campeche dyewood was logwood (palo de tinte), a different plant.

sources.citation: Juan Juárez Moreno, Corsarios y piratas en Veracruz y Campeche (Escuela de Estudios Hispano-Americanos, 1972).
Peter Gerhard, The Southeast Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: Conquest of the Itzá at Nojpetén
properties.label: Nojpetén 1697
properties.description: For 170 years the Itzá Maya kingdom on Lake Petén Itzá, in the forests between Yucatán and Guatemala, stayed independent and sheltered refugees from Spanish rule. Martín de Ursúa, governor of Yucatán, had a road cut south from Campeche from 1695 and attacked the island capital of Nojpetén by boat. Its fall ended the last independent Maya kingdom; the site is now the town of Flores, Guatemala.

sources.citation: Grant D. Jones, The Conquest of the Last Maya Kingdom (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Peter Gerhard, The Southeast Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: The Tzeltal revolt of Cancuc
properties.label: Cancuc 1712
properties.description: After a young woman, María de la Candelaria, reported visions of the Virgin at Cancuc, Tzeltal, Tzotzil and Ch'ol towns of the Chiapas highlands rose against Spanish priests, officials and tribute, forming their own church and army. Troops sent by the Audiencia of Guatemala, which governed Chiapas, crushed the rising by early 1713.

sources.citation: Kevin Gosner, Soldiers of the Virgin: The Moral Economy of a Colonial Maya Rebellion (University of Arizona Press, 1992).
Peter Gerhard, The Southeast Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).
